reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
[Editorial Note: Please see the final page of this file for the attached figure]
Thank you for addressing my review and for your thorough response. I am satisfied with the manuscript revisions regarding statistical significance and the treatment of secondaries.
Concern remains regarding a fundamental assumption of a direct and obvious correlation between regolith depth and age. Since my review, Bart (2025) has published a review of observational evidence of regolith depth from diverse sources collected over the last several decades (including those cited in the rebuttal to my previous review). Bart (2025) demonstrates that the observations of regolith depth do not support the depth-age hypothesis. To illustrate this point, in an attached figure, I plot regolith depth versus mare age for the CE'5 regolith depth estimates from this manuscript, two of the data sources included in Bart (2025) (Bart et al. (2011) and Shkuratov & Bondarenko (2001)), and a recently published assessment of regolith depth evolution on crater ejecta (Thanker & Neish 2025). This figure includes error bars, which compound the poor statistical correlation between depth and time identified by Bart (2025). The data show no positive correlation between age and regolith depth. A straight line could fit through all of the data in the figure, including the CE'5 data. Observations are relatively sparse for surfaces younger than 2.5 Ga, and the 70-cm radar scattering model underpinning the Shkuratov & Bondarenko (2001) regolith depth measurements has unresolved issues (Campbell 2002), but the available data do not support a clear relationship between regolith depth and age, even for these young surfaces.
The apparent lack of correlation between observed regolith depth and mare age must be reconciled with the statement in the revised manuscript: "Therefore, regolith thickness is statistically linked to surface age and can serve as a robust indicator of lunar impact history, particularly for a young lunar surface, as supported by both observational and modeling results." (L72-73)
I agree that impacts likely dominate regolith generation, and I agree that the properties of the study landing region are relatively uniform. In light of these agreements and having read the same assertions that were cited in the rebuttal, like the direct quote from the Lunar Sourcebook, I was surprised by the lack of depth-age correlation when assessing the sum of regolith depth observations collected over the last few decades; however, given the apparent poor correlation between observed regolith depth and age in the mare, it is clear that a direct relationship between flux, surface age, and regolith depth cannot be taken as a given.
Consider discussing the issues with the depth-age hypothesis, focusing on the unique case/location presented in this manuscript, and including more of the material written in the thorough rebuttal to my previous review, particularly concerning the representativeness of the P58 unit. An explicit argument would strengthen the manuscript that while the story of regolith depth and its evolution is complicated and poorly correlated with surface age when viewed across multipule mare (e.g., Bart 2025, Chertok et al. 2023), we can use models to assess individual locations, like Hirabayashi et al. (2018) did for Apollo 15 and this manuscript does for the CE'5 site, because we expect the effects of factors like protolith properties, local large crater ejecta, development of a regolith buffer that is subsequently mixed etc., to be within the scope of model parameterization.

The manuscript, titled “Increased Small Impactor Flux on the Moon as Inferred from Regolith Thickness at the Chang’E-5 Region” by Mingwei Zhang et al., maintains a clear and exciting research goal: use the regolith thickness distribution at the Chang'E-5 region to infer the impact flux rate at the recent two billion years on the Moon. Is it truly sufficient to have two layers model (LTREM) to explain the observed regolith thickness distribution? How the two layers regolith model can dynamically capture the random nature of cratering process and complexity of interaction between regolith growth and compression, as well as target properties, has to be tested an quantified against more sites.

Thanks for your constructive comment. We agree with the reviewer that “while the story of regolith depth and its evolution is complicated and poorly correlated with surface age when viewed across multiple mare, we can use models to assess individual locations”. Our response is structured into four parts: (1) the attached figure, (2) evaluation of the thickness–age relationship based on observations, (3) factors influencing this relationship, and (4) the representativeness and uniqueness of the CE-5 region.
1. On the attached figure
Thanks for providing the figure and we appreciate this effort to integrate existing results. In this figure, the regolith thickness does not show a clear correlation with age. However, we want to emphasize a few limitations of this compilation. First, the statistical metrics are not consistent: mean and standard deviation for Shkuratov & Bondarenko (2001) and Thanker & Neish (2025), whereas median and min/max values for Bart et al. (2011). Second, there are inherent systematic differences among different studies due to varying data sources, methodologies, and underlying assumptions. For example, the crater morphology method is based on the strength discontinuity between regolith and bedrock (Bart et al. 2011), whereas radar observations rely on the differences in their dielectrical properties (Shkuratov & Bondarenko 2001). Besides, regolith growth on ejecta deposits (Thanker & Neish 2025) may not be directly comparable with that on mare basalts, because fine-grained materials within ejecta blankets may themselves already be part of the regolith. All these issues could affect the interpretation of the plotted trends.
2. Regolith thickness vs. age from multi-source observations
To systematically evaluate the correlation between regolith thickness and age, we analyzed regolith thickness estimated from radar observations, microwave radiometer measurements, and the crater morphology method, respectively. Then, two statistical tests—the Spearman rank correlation and the Mann-Kendall test—were applied to these results. The Spearman rank correlation is a non-parametric test that assesses the strength and direction of the monotonic relationship between two variables, without assuming a linear relationship or normal distribution. The correlation coefficient (ρ: –1 to 1) indicates how strongly two sets of ranks are correlated (Spearman 1987). The Mann-Kendall test is a non-parametric statistical test used to detect the presence of a monotonic trend in a time series without requiring any particular distribution for the data (Hussain & Mahmud 2019). For both methods, the p value represents the probability of observing the data under the null hypothesis, with a small p value indicating a statistically significant monotonic correlation.
2.1 Radar observations
Using the Earth-based 70-cm Arecibo radar data, Shkuratov and Bondarenko (2001) inverted the regolith thickness over the lunar nearside based on a multiple scattering model of radar waves. We georeferenced the regolith thickness map of Shkuratov and Bondarenko (2001) with the mare basalts dated by Hiesinger et al. (Supplementary Fig. 1). We then calculated the mean regolith thickness within each basalt unit containing more than 100 pixels (400–2500 km2), as shown in Supplementary Fig. 2. The blue line shows the prediction of the analytical regolith growth model (Zhang et al. 2023a), which is applicable for surface younger than 3.5 Ga due to different earlier impactor populations (Xie et al. 2021).
For all the dots, the Spearman rank correlation yielded a ρ value of 0.12 with a p-value of 0.09, indicating no significant monotonic relationship between regolith thickness and age. Consistently, the Mann-Kendall test detected no significant trend with a p-value of 0.08. We further performed an analysis on basalts whose target properties showed no significant anomalies (the red dots), defined as rock abundance values falling within one standard deviation in Supplementary Fig. 7. The results also indicate no significant trend.
In conclusion, the regolith thickness derived from Shkuratov and Bondarenko (2001) shows no correlation with age. However, this lack of correlation is likely due to problems with the radar data calibration and inversion method (Campbell 2002; Fa and Wieczorek 2012). A detailed discussion including the data calibration, radar scattering model, and polarization properties can be found in the Introduction of Fa and Wieczorek (2012) (second-to-last paragraph of page 772), and is not repeated here.

The global distribution of lunar regolith thickness was derived from the 3 GHz brightness temperature observed by CE-1 microwave radiometer (Fa and Jin 2010; Supplementary Fig. 3). Similarly, we calculated the mean regolith thickness within each basalt unit containing more than 10 pixels (~9000 km2 at the equator), as shown in Supplementary Fig. 4.
For all the dots, the Spearman rank correlation yielded a ρ value of 0.40 with a p-value of 1.2´10-6, indicating a statistically significant moderate correlation between regolith thickness and age. Consistently, the Mann-Kendall test detected an increasing trend with a p-value of 1.0´10-6. The red dots represent the basalts whose target properties showed no significant anomalies and the statistical results for these red dots also indicate a moderate correlation between regolith thickness and age.

In summary, the regolith thickness estimated from microwave radiometer measurements (Fa and Jin, 2010) and the crater morphology method (Bart et al., 2011) shows a moderate correlation with age, whereas the thickness estimated from radar observations (Shkuratov and Bondarenko, 2001) shows no such correlation. As already mentioned, there are several issues with the radar-based method of Shkuratov and Bondarenko (2001); therefore, we consider regolith thickness and age to show an overall moderate statistical correlation. Our statement that “regolith thickness is statistically linked to surface age” is based on the statistical tests described above, and does not imply that older surfaces necessarily have thicker regolith than younger surfaces. In fact, we agree with the reviewer’s perspective and the difference lies only in the wording of our description.
In the revision, we discussed this correlation thoroughly in the main text and point out that, while there is a moderate statistical correlation, some regions clearly deviate from this trend, in order to avoid any misinterpretation (see L81–91). We also added Supplementary Text 1 and Figs. 1–5 providing the regolith thickness obtained from radar observations, microwave radiometer measurements and crater morphology.
3. Reasons for the variability in regolith thickness
Since lunar regolith is primarily formed by impacts (e.g., Mckay et al. 1991), its thickness within a given geological unit is expected to increase over time. However, the regolith thicknesses in mare units with different ages across the Moon exhibit considerable variation, and their correlation with age is not particularly strong (Supplementary Figs. 2, 4 and 5). This may be attributed to the following four factors.
3.1 Limitations associated with the data and methods
For regolith thickness, radar-derived estimates are strongly influenced by the choice of radar wave scattering model and radar data radiometric calibration error (Shkuratov and Bondarenko 2001), which lead to large errors for regolith thickness inversion (Campbell 2002; Fa and Wieczorek 2012). In contrast, the crater morphology method is based on impact experiments (Quaide and Oberbeck 1968; Oberbeck and Quaide 1967, 1968) and further supported by numerical simulations (Senft and Stewart 2007), making it relatively more reliable.
For ages of mare basalts, crater-counting results reported by Hiesinger et al. can differ substantially from sample-based ages. For example, the P58 unit was previously estimated to be ~1.3 Ga by crater counting (Hiesinger et al. 2011), whereas isotopic dating of the CE-5 samples yields an age of ~2.0 Ga (Li et al. 2021). For the CE-3 landing region, Hiesinger et al. (2011) estimated an age of 2.96 Ga, whereas Qian et al. (2023) reported an age of 1.4 Ga, both of which used crater counting method. Without isotopic dating, it remains difficult to assess its accurate age. Similar discrepancies are expected in other mare units as well.
The errors in both regolith thickness and age estimates can weaken the apparent correlation between them.
3.2 Variation of target property
Recent observations of both rocky crater populations and surface rock abundances indicate that mechanical properties vary substantially across different mare basalt units (e.g., Elder et al., 2023; Chertok et al., 2023). The strength and bulk density of the target material can influence crater sizes and thus affect regolith production rates (e.g., Zhang et al., 2023a). This issue has been discussed in the reviewer’s comments and our previous response.
3.3 Random nature of large impacts
Lunar regolith is primarily formed by local small impacts but is also influenced by exotic ejecta deposits (e.g., Mckay et al. 1991; Xie et al. 2020a). Numerous small craters can be considered spatially uniform, whereas large craters are relatively rare and exhibit highly stochastic spatial patterns. Areas affected by ejecta and secondary craters from large impacts tend to have thicker regolith. The spatial randomness and temporal episodicity of large impacts result in regolith thicknesses that do not increase steadily with time across different geological units (e.g., crater Xu Guangqi in the simulation area and crater Copernicus outside the area).
3.4 Buffering trend in regolith growth
As regolith thickens, small impactors merely overturn the existing regolith layer, while only larger impactors capable of penetrating the pre-existing regolith can fracture the underlying substrate and produce new regolith. As a result, regolith growth rate decreases over time and is limited in older surfaces.
These factors are mentioned in the introduction section (see L92–95) and detailed in the Supplementary Text 2.
4. Regolith evolution in the CE-5 region
As suggested by the reviewer, though regolith thickness and age lack a strong correlation across the Moon, it is feasible to conduct a detailed modeling of the regolith evolution at individual appropriate regions, where the influences of the above factors can be minimized as much as possible. The CE-5 landing region is such a unique location, providing an unprecedented opportunity to estimate the impact flux.
4.1 The high-resolution imagery acquired by the descent camera enabled a reliable estimate of the regional distribution of regolith thickness. The precise isotopic age of 2.03±0.004 Ga avoids the large dating uncertainties associated with crater counting (addressing factor 3.1).
4.2 Spectroscopic observations show that the CE-5 landing region of several tens of kilometers across exhibits uniform target characteristics (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 4). Both the frequency of rocky craters and statistics of rock abundance indicate that the P58 unit is representative of typical mare basalts used to construct the NPF (Supplementary Fig. 7). This was explained in detail in our prior response (addressing factor 3.2).
4.3 As the youngest radiometrically dated mare unit, the CE-5 region has a relatively simple geological evolution history. The source craters contributing to regolith generation at the CE-5 region have been thoroughly documented. By taking these source craters as model inputs, the contribution from large impacts has been explicitly incorporated (addressing factor 3.3).
Besides, the regolith growth in such a young surface is less influenced by the buffering effect (addressing factor 3.4).
In the revision, we emphasized the feasibility of inferring the impact flux from regolith evolution modeling at the CE-5 landing site. See L151–166.
In conclusion, we agree with the reviewer that the existing observations do not support a strong correlation between regolith thickness and age. We rephrased our statement regarding the correlation, discussed the potential reasons for the variation of regolith thickness across the Moon, and explained why it is feasible to estimate the impact flux from the regolith thickness at the CE-5 landing region. We explained these issues in the introduction (see L71–65, L120–139, L151–166) and provided more detailed descriptions in Supplementary Texts 1 and 2 and Supplementary Figs. 1–5.
Answers to Reviewer 3
We appreciate the reviewer’s evaluation on our manuscript. In the revision, we carefully revised our manuscript according to the reviewer’s comments. Specifically, we explained the validity of using a two-layer model and performed additional statistical analyses to support our conclusions. A point-by-point response is provided below.
Comments from the reviewer are in black, and line numbers in the reviewer’s comments refer to those in our original manuscript.
Replies from the authors are in red, and line numbers in our replies refer to those in the track change revision References are provided at the end of the file.
Major comments
Q1. However, the observed drilling core and seismic data shows a more complicated layer structure of regolith, instead of the underlying assumption that uses two layers model to classify the crater morphology. How the Zhang et al. model tackles this complexity (regolith dynamics and interaction with cratering) is unclear in the current manuscript.
• We acknowledge that the both the Apollo and Luna core samples revealed a complex layered structure within the regolith, characterized primarily by variations in grain size, composition, maturity, and noble gas concentrations. However, this microscale internal structure does not impact the method we use to estimate regolith thickness, which is based on the mechanical properties of the regolith and the underlying bedrock.
• We do not agree with the referee’s comment that seismic data indicates a more complicated layer structure of regolith. Actually, the Apollo seismic experiments showed a relatively homogeneous regolith structure: “P-wave velocities measured in regolith at the Apollo landing sites are very low and uniform and range from 92 to 114 m/sec” (Carrier et al. 1991, Lunar Sourcebook, p.516 in chapter 9). The uniform P-wave velocity within the regolith, along with its increase at the base of the regolith layer, suggests a homogeneous regolith overlying bedrock. This seismic characteristic is the basis for estimating regolith thickness (see Nakamura et al., 1975, The Moon, pp. 57–66).
• The two-layer target model (i.e., a loose granular layer atop a cohesive substrate) has been validated through both impact experiments and numerical simulations. The most widely used method for estimating regolith thickness—small crater morphology—was developed through impact experiments on a regolith-bedrock two-layer target (Quaide and Oberbeck, 1968; Oberbeck and Quaide, 1967, 1968). The four observed morphological types of small lunar craters were successfully reproduced in numerical impact cratering simulations using a two-layer structure (e.g., Senft and Stewart, 2007). In addition, comparisons with regolith thickness measurements from lunar seismic experiments have demonstrated that this method is reliable and largely unaffected by internal layering within the regolith (e.g., 11
Di et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021). Therefore, the two-layer model can serve as an effective approximation of the lunar surface (i.e., regolith-bedrock) and has long been employed in estimating regolith thickness. We explained this in L468–472 in the revision.
Q2. In addition, the crater population in Chang’E 5 site is fitted with Neukum function and seems relatively consistent with isotopically dated ages of mare basalt (2 Ga). In the current manuscript, it is not clear that how the crater population with increased impact flux in the model differs from the observed crater population.
We discussed this in L333–346 in our original manuscript.
The diameter ranges of impact craters in Yue et al. (2022) and in our study are different. In Yue et al. (2022), craters with diameters >200 m were used to fit the chronology function. In contrast, our study revealed an increased impact flux for sub-hectometer small craters (<100 m), a diameter range to which regolith thickness is most sensitive (see Extended Data Fig. 5). Within this diameter range, the rapid degradation of impact craters produces a bias between the observed (e.g., the Neukum production function) and the actual crater production.

Thank you for the suggestion. In the revision, we defined the self-limiting process and the buffering trend in regolith growth (See L68–73). Due to the self-limiting nature of regolith formation, its growth is sensitive to impact flux primarily on geologically young lunar surfaces. This is why we selected the CE-5 landing region for this study, as it is the youngest isotopically dated mare basalt unit.

The percentages reported here are derived from Fig. 3d, where the contributions to regolith formation from the observed, invisible, and secondary craters were recorded. As a large number of craters form in LTREM, the bedrock is shattered and excavated, and the regolith is deposited and transported, which is a dynamic process. Different parameters primarily affect the total regolith thickness, while the relative contribution percentages remain largely stable. The 1σ uncertainty is 0.1%. reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I appreciate that responses to my reviews have been comprehensive. However, a core problem remains. The manuscript does not present a convincing argument that it is currently feasible to predict flux based on regolith depth, as significant and incorrect assumptions are made regarding the relationship between regolith depth and time, leaving significant uncertainties unaddressed.
The timescales examined by statistical methods to correlate age and regolith depth using microwave and crater morphology (>3 Ga) are not relevant to the subtle and recent variations in flux discussed in this manuscript. The data analyzed for the microwave correlation spans ages from approximately 1 Ga to 4 Ga, with an apparent uptick after 3.5 Ga. Similarly, the crater morphology method (Bart et al., 2011) also spans the 2.5 to 3.5 Ga period. I suspect that the statistical correlation results from including regolith depths for surfaces older than 3 Ga, where the impact rate increases significantly. The correlation between regolith depth and age (and recent impact flux) will only be convincing if the data examined are within the relatively flat 1 to 3 Ga timescale.
Consider performing these statistical analyses of regolith depth versus surface age over the limited timescale of 1-3 Ga to assess whether a definitive depth-age-flux correlation exists for relatively young surfaces (like the CE'5 landing site).
The statistical uncertainty in the link between the model and observed regolith depth must also be reflected in the uncertainty in modeled regolith depht and the flux implied by the difference between the model and observations (e.g., Fig. 4). In the response to reviewers, section "1. Two-sigma confidence interval", a modeled regolith depth of 2.9±0.14 m is reported; however, the reported error does not account for the uncertainty we find between the observed regolith depth and model predictions versus time at relevant timesclaes. A larger uncertainty in the model-predicted regolith depth will result in significantly different statistics and confidence when compared to the observed depth at the CE'5 landing site. Without an analysis of model uncertainty, it is unclear whether the possibly significant uncertainty invalidates predictions regarding an uptick in flux.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Dear Zhang et al.,
This reviewer is pleased by the overall context and revised edits provided by Zhang et al titled “Increased Small Impactor Flux on the Moon as Inferred from Regolith Thickness at the Chang’E-5 Region”. This reviewer would like to thank authors for making their regolith evolution model more understandable and thinking about statistical interpretation from variety sources of the observational constrained regolith thickness dataset. The hypothesis regarding the relationship between the surface age and the regolith growth remain testable, requiring more research work on this topic. Zhang et al., also have provided sufficient content on addressing the effects of primary small impacts on the regolith growth model. As the authors proposed the primary small impacts are dominant source of regolith growth at the Chang’E 5 landing site, that is, this population is currently invisible due to the crater degradation and crater equilibrium, as a result, uncertainties concerning the size frequency distribution (~<85 meter in diameter) are high and have to be constrained from the additional information such as the observed glass spherule ages, boulder distribution, and LROC impact flash observations. The authors have shown a vast room of improving understanding of primary small crater population as their modeling under five types of production functions (in combination of magnitude of increased impact rate and corresponding crater size range) can match the observed regolith thickness. However, this reviewer still feels unclear about the fragmentation of bedrock part in the regolith evolution model though the authors have provided quite some work regarding the working principles of the model. For example, the regolith is defined as breakdown of bedrock and created via either ejecta blanket or breccias lens. This should be fine until the surface is covered by the craters and more subsequent craters in next time step. How does the model handle the surface covered by loosely regolith materials? This is back to the original point from this reviewer regarding the compaction part of the model. Also, this reviewer strongly suggests the authors, if available, have some general discussion on how types of crater morphology reflects the underlying regolith layer structure (the experimental study in Quaide and Oberbeck, 1968). As the backbone of the manuscript is based on the relationship between regolith thickness and crater morphology, it would be great for supplementing this plot if it is available or the analysis is not too challenging. Finally, this reviewer has minor comments for the authors to improve the manuscript context regarding the geological history at Chang’E 5 landing site from Evans et al., (2018) and Fu et al., (2021). Please see the annotated PDF of the author’s revised manuscript (highlighted in purple color with comment box).
Warm regards,
Ya Huei Huang

reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
Review of “Increased Small Impactor 1 Flux on the Moon as Inferred from Regolith Thickness at the Chang’E-5 Region”
Summary and evaluation
This paper makes the case that the regolith thickness in the Chang’E-5 landing region demands a higher impact flux than is found in the standard chronology model. The argument for this is based on a coupled regolith and terrain evolution model. If correct, this enhanced impact flux is important.
A [very] major strength of this paper is the care with which the regolith evolution modeling has been considered – this is absolutely state-of-the-art and will be a valuable addition to the literature. The main [minor] weak element I’d raise is that this paper is essentially trying to make a fairly significant claim based on this model by comparing it to a kind-of-messy single data point (i.e., the regolith thickness on C’E-5 surface e.g. Fig. 1b). This could lead us astray if either the thickness data has unexpected systematics (i.e., I think the traditional regolith-thickness derivation using morphology were developed on larger craters), or if the model functional behavior or parameterizations are incorrect.
Overall, however, I think the real methodological innovations of this work outweigh any concerns I have about the applications of the model, so I would argue for acceptance after minor revisions at the author’s discretion. I hope the authors might explore additional applications of their model later and give a few ideas for this in my comments (e.g. #3).
General comments:
1) I have been added as a reviewer in a later round. Reading the back and forth in the rebuttal document, I see that the authors ran into an earlier reviewer skepticism regarding the notion that regolith thickens with time and that older units have thicker regolith. I agree with the authors here: it’s a noisy relationship, but one that both (a) is likely to hold from first principles, and (b) looks empirically supported, from a variety of observations. In fact, I think we would be surprised if the relationship was stronger (in agreement with Line 88-95) given (a) the inherent variability of the relevant processes, (b) the relatively narrow age of most mare surface area, and (c) the buffering effect.
2) I see that, in at least the original iteration of the analysis, the Neukum production function was extrapolated to sizes <10m in diameter (e.g. ExData Fig 6), which is formally below where it was defined. I think it is extremely plausible that the slope of the PF steepens below some size because of the known steeper PF of small grains (Grun 1985). Regardless of the details here (whether steepening happens at 2 m or 20 m), I do not think it alters the results much. Craters in this regime mostly garden (like secondaries) rather than increase regolith thickness, but it is something worth considering.
3) I think everywhere this paper talks about regolith thickness, it is talking about the median, but there is potentially more of a handle on the relevant parameters if it was possible to invert for the full regolith thickness distribution. I would admit that the available data to do this might not be confident enough, but I would encourage further thinking on that path.
Specific comments:
Line 46: The survival time has some implicit ‘visibility threshold’ built in, see Minton et al 2019; Fassett et al. 2022. Fassett et al 2022 also calculate slightly longer survival times than given here. Note that in looking at Fig. 2, I think the authors’ visibility threshold (ie how degraded a crater has to be to be recognized) is lower than mine.
Line 63. Little to no regolith is present. The cited Head and Wilson paper disagrees
(https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2020GL088334). I tend to think the authors are probably right (although regardless the first 50cm-1m of growth isn’t that important because it grows quickly, due to the lack of a significant buffering effect).
Line 81. I know this paragraph was largely added at the behest of the earlier reviewer, but it feels distracting here. Is there a place later in the paper where it logically could flow better? I think I agree with everything here.
Line 400. Was this supposed to be a reference to supplementary figure 10-11?
Line 570-574. I’m not surprised that the diffusivity has negligible effect on the median, though the use of a constant, lower-than-applicable effective diffusivity for big craters (~50-100m+) potentially causes an under-thickening of regolith in their interiors? I think the model is showing this behavior by looking rougher at the sub-saturated sizes in Fig. 3, 1500 Myr, than the real Moon.
Line 618. Is it transient crater depth, or the whole shape? Curious: Does you model intentionally seek to conserve mass/volume?
Line 702. It would be nice if the code for LTREM were made available for reproducibility reasons.
Line 953. I don’t think I understand Fig. 1b. Why is it allowable for this curve to not be monotonically increasing? As I read this, the series for concentric craters would predict less area with thickness <6.5m than <5m, which doesn’t seem logical. For reference, I think this figure is a little like observational data akin to Fig. 6 of Hirabayashi et al. 2018 (though perhaps with axes switched). I would find it useful to have this translated into a best estimate for the regolith cfd/sfd (areal fraction with thickness <X or =X or >X or whatever).
Line 991. This figure is pretty cool…nice work.
Suppl. Figure 2, 4. I’ll note that these look sort of like Vanga et al.’s Fig 3 median regolith thicknesses, though probably with some difference in the values.

Answers to Reviewer 2
We appreciate the reviewer’s comments on our manuscript. A point-by-point response is provided below.
Comments from the reviewer are in black, and line numbers in the reviewer’s comments refer to those in our original manuscript.
Replies from the authors are in red, and line numbers in our replies refer to those in the track change revision. 
Q1. I appreciate that responses to my reviews have been comprehensive. However, a core problem remains. The manuscript does not present a convincing argument that it is currently feasible to predict flux based on regolith depth, as significant and incorrect assumptions are made regarding the relationship between regolith depth and time, leaving significant uncertainties unaddressed.

The data analyzed for the microwave correlation spans ages from approximately 1 Ga to 4 Ga, with an apparent uptick after 3.5 Ga. Similarly, the crater morphology method (Bart et al., 2011) also spans the 2.5 to 3.5 Ga period. I suspect that the statistical correlation results from including regolith depths for surfaces older than 3 Ga, where the impact rate increases significantly. The correlation between regolith depth and age (and recent impact flux) will only be convincing if the data examined are within the relatively flat 1 to 3 Ga timescale.
Consider performing these statistical analyses of regolith depth versus surface age over the limited timescale of 1-3 Ga to assess whether a definitive depth-age-flux correlation exists for relatively young surfaces (like the CE-5 landing site).
As noted by Reviewer #5, the correlation between regolith thickness and age holds from first principles, and it is also supported by observations as shown in Supplementary Figs. 2, 4, and 5. We understand the reviewer’s concern that this correlation may be obscured by other factors, especially for surfaces younger than 3 Ga. This has been discussed in the manuscript (L76–78 and Supplementary Text 2), and we agree that the statistical correlation is not particularly strong due to (1) uncertainties in the estimates of age and regolith thickness, (2) variations in target properties, and (3) the stochastic nature of large impact events. However, our goal is not to demonstrate a universal correlation between regolith thickness and age across all the mare units (<3 Ga). It is exactly because of the noise present in the global observations that we chose the CE-5 region for this study. Owing to the unique geological setting, the returned samples, and the availability of high-resolution data at the CE-5 landing site, the uncertainties in both age and regolith thickness, the effects of target property variations, and the spatiotemporal randomness of large impacts, are substantially reduced. Therefore, it is feasible to infer the impact flux from the regolith thickness in the CE-5 region. Please see our prior response for more detail regarding the uniqueness of the CE-5 region.
Q2. The statistical uncertainty in the link between the model and observed regolith depth must also be reflected in the uncertainty in modeled regolith depth and the flux implied by the difference between the model and observations (e.g., Fig. 4). In the response to reviewers, section "1. Two-sigma confidence interval", a modeled regolith depth of 2.9±0.14 m is reported; however, the reported error does not account for the uncertainty we find between the observed regolith depth and model predictions versus time at relevant time scales. A larger uncertainty in the model-predicted regolith depth will result in significantly different statistics and confidence when compared to the observed depth at the CE'5 landing site. Without an analysis of model uncertainty, it is unclear whether the possibly significant uncertainty invalidates predictions regarding an uptick in flux.
The uncertainty we find between the observed regolith thickness and predictions from an analytical model versus time represents arises from a series of factors described in Supplementary Text 2 (see also our reply to Q1), which differs from the model/observation uncertainty at the CE-5 region in this study. In such a carefully selected study area, the uncertainties associated with age and regolith thickness measurements are substantially reduced, the target exhibits no anomalous mechanical properties, the buffering effect is relatively weak, and the major source craters have been thoroughly identified and incorporated into our model. Therefore, the overall uncertainty at the CE-5 landing site is relatively small and has been adequately reported (3.6±0.3 m for observation and 2.9±0.14 m for simulation).
Answers to Reviewer 3
We appreciate the reviewer’s comments on our manuscript. In the revision, we carefully revised our manuscript. A point-by-point response is provided below.
Comments from the reviewer are in black, and line numbers in the reviewer’s comments refer to those in our original manuscript.
Replies from the authors are in red, and line numbers in our replies refer to those in the track change revision.
Q1. However, this reviewer still feels unclear about the fragmentation of bedrock part in the regolith evolution model though the authors have provided quite some work regarding the working principles of the model. For example, the regolith is defined as breakdown of bedrock and created via either ejecta blanket or breccias lens. This should be fine until the surface is covered by the craters and more subsequent craters in next time step. How does the model handle the surface covered by loosely regolith materials? This is back to the original point from this reviewer regarding the compaction part of the model.
These methodological details have been described in our previous studies (Section 4.1 in Zhang et al., 2023a, JGR-Planets, and Section 2.2 in Zhang et al., 2023b, JGR-Planets). In brief, we estimate the volume of fractured bedrock based on the geometry of the final and transient crater profiles, rather than modeling the physical fracturing process. This approach is applicable to various preimpact target conditions (including regolith-covered surfaces), and any compaction or expansion is inherently incorporated through the crater topographic profile. The treatment adopted here differs from the porosity compaction approach used in the reviewer’s recent study (Huang et al., Nat. Geosci. 15, 531–535, 2022). In the revision, we clarified the principle underlying the simulation of bedrock fragmentation and provided a more precise reference to our previous work (Section 2.2 in Zhang et al., 2023b). See L522–526.
Q2. Also, this reviewer strongly suggests the authors, if available, have some general discussion on how types of crater morphology reflects the underlying regolith layer structure (the experimental study in Quaide and Oberbeck, 1968). As the backbone of the manuscript is based on the relationship between regolith thickness and crater morphology, it would be great for supplementing this plot if it is available or the analysis is not too challenging.
Thanks for the suggestion. We described the relationship between regolith thickness and crater morphology in the section “Regolith Thickness Estimation from Small Crater Morphology” in Methods. The underlying principle is straightforward: a normal crater forms when the ratio of crater diameter (D) to regolith thickness (T) <4±0.1; a concentric crater forms when D/T >9±0.6; a central mound or flat-bottomed crater forms when 4±0.1< D/T <9±0.6. See the diagram below.
On this basis, the percentage of fresh craters with different morphological types (Supplementary Fig. 8) could be converted to the area fraction of regolith thickness (Fig. 1b). For example, in the diameter range D_i, the percentage of concentric craters is 90%, then 90% of the area has a regolith thickness less than D_i/(9±0.6).
The crater morphology method has been widely used for regolith thickness estimation in the literature (e.g., Fa et al., 2014, JGR-Planets, 10.1002/2013JE004604; Yang et al., 2021, GRL, 10.1029/2021GL095537; Xie et al., 2021 NA, 10.1038/s41550-020-01241-8; Joulaud et al., 2024, Space Sci Rev, 10.1007/s11214-024-01101-1), and a diagram can be found in Fig. 2 of Zhang et al., 2023a. Therefore, we provided the relevant references and explained the method within the text without adding a diagram in the manuscript. See L426–441. For clarification, we added the reference to Supplementary Fig. 8 in the revision.
Minor comments
Q3. L161. May want to be careful with this. Fu et al., (2022) proposed possible non-mare basalt in Chang'E 5 landing site, as well as few quasi-circular mass anomaly from gravity data analysis (Evans et al., (2018). After all, the homogeneous layer of the topmost surface might not be accurate for underlying geological setting. Reference:
Evans et al., (2018) https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2017JE005421
Fu et al., (2021) https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2020JE006797
Thanks for the references. The proportion of non-mare materials in the CE-5 regolith is only ~5%, as supported by our modeling results (Fig. 4b) and laboratory measurements (Wu et al., 2024, Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences, 52, 159–194), which align with Fu et al. (2021). The contamination of exotic material and the mass anomaly do not influence the basalt mechanical properties in this study. Therefore, we prefer not to change here.
Q4. L173. “that are widespread on the lunar surface” Consider to delete it.
We deleted “that are widespread”. See L146.
Q5. L233–235. Method section seems lacking of description for fragmentation of bedrocks.
Please see our response to Q1.
Q6. L433–442. Quaide and Oberbeck (1968) was the first to extrapolate the regolith thickness using two layers model, in which is based on the correlation between features of craters versus the apparent diameter of a crater and the regolith thickness. This reviewer has two suggestions:
1.It might not be straightforward for readers to estimate regolith thickness. Though in the following text the authors explained pros and cons from the types of crater morphology. Please consider to add simple text regarding the regolith thickness estimate. For example, Figure 10 in Quaide and Oberbeck (1968) is an illustrative example.
2. Please consider to provide your data and plot similar to Figure 8, D_F/D_A vs. D_A/t in Quaide and Oberbeck (1968) study if it is available.
Thanks for the suggestions. There are two approaches for regolith thickness estimation proposed by Quaide & Oberbeck (1968)
1. Based on the diameter of the crater interior feature and the crater rim-to-rim diameter (D_F/D_A vs. D_A/t, as mentioned in suggestion #2).
2. Based on the size-frequency distribution of craters with four morphological types.
Please note that the reviewer’s suggestion applies to Approach 1. In this study, we employed the Approach 2, which utilizes the relative proportions of crater types and does not require D_F. For an illustrative example, please see the diagram in our response to Q2. The text regarding the regolith thickness estimate can be found at L426–441. We also present our data in a format similar to Fig. 2 in Oberbeck and Quaide, 1967, JGR, 10.1029/JZ072i018p04697 (Supplementary Fig. 8). In the revision, we provided the reference to our previous work for a more detailed description of the workflow. See L432.

Thanks for the suggestion. We agree with the reviewer that the full regolith thickness distribution carries more information. We provide the spatial distribution of the modeled regolith thickness in Fig. 4a and the probability density functions (PDFs) in Fig. 5a. To better characterize the overall features of the long-tailed distribution pattern and to facilitate comparison with observations, we adopted the median as a representative measure.

(https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2020GL088334). I tend to think the authors are probably right (although regardless the first 50cm-1m of growth isn’t that important because it grows quickly, due to the lack of a significant buffering effect).
We agree with the reviewer. We cited Head and Wilson paper mainly because of their introduction of the concepts of impact flux trend and buffering trend, which are relevant for our modeling framework. In the revision, we cited McKay et al. 1991, Lunar Sourcebook here.
Q7. Line 81. I know this paragraph was largely added at the behest of the earlier reviewer, but it feels distracting here. Is there a place later in the paper where it logically could flow better? I think I agree with everything here.
We agree with the reviewer. In the revision, we simplified this text and moved it forward to improve the overall logic. See L73–78. We also added a brief summary at the end of Supplementary Text 2.
Q8. Line 400. Was this supposed to be a reference to supplementary figure 10-11?
Yes. We added the reference in the revision. See L367.
Q9. Line 570-574. I’m not surprised that the diffusivity has negligible effect on the median, though the use of a constant, lower-than-applicable effective diffusivity for big craters (~50-100m+) potentially causes an under-thickening of regolith in their interiors? I think the model is showing this behavior by looking rougher at the sub-saturated sizes in Fig. 3, 1500 Myr, than the real Moon.
Yes, this is an insightful comment. Using a uniform equivalent diffusivity across the entire simulation area indeed leads to an underestimation of the degradation rate for large craters. This could make a difference to the spatial distribution pattern of regolith thickness. However, since degradation mainly redistributes regolith rather than producing new regolith, it does not affect the median regolith thickness in any significant manner, as the reviewer noted.
In future work, we plan to update the model by allowing the degradation rate to vary across regions according to local slope to better simulate the degradation of craters with different sizes (larger craters generally contain more steeply sloped areas). We described the limitation of the equivalent diffusivity in the revision. See L550–556.
Q10. Line 618. Is it transient crater depth, or the whole shape? Curious: Does you model intentionally seek to conserve mass/volume?
It is the whole shape of the transient crater that influences regolith thickness. However, since a bowl-shaped cavity is commonly used to represent transient crater geometry (e.g., Melosh 1989; Hirabayashi et al., 2018, JGR-Planets), the crater depth becomes the key parameter. In this study, we varied the transient crater shape by assigning different transient crater depths (L537–538). For accuracy, we refer to the transient crater depth here, though both descriptions are correct.
The volume change during impact cratering process is considered based on the observed topographic profiles of 99 fresh lunar craters (extracted by Cai and Fa 2020, doi.org/10.1029/2020JE006429; Yang et al. 2021, doi.org/10.1029/2021GL095537). As shown in Fig. 6d in Zhang et al. 2023a (JGR-Planets, 128, e2023JE007850), kilometer-sized craters exhibit a negative volume change, while the volume for craters smaller than ~100 m is nearly conserved. The volume-neutral nature of sub-hectometer craters ensures that numerous small craters that do not penetrate the existing regolith layer neither add nor remove regolith in an area. We clarified this in the revision. See L514–517.
Q11. Line 702. It would be nice if the code for LTREM were made available for reproducibility reasons.
We plan to release the model as software in the future. It takes some time because of user interaction design, docstrings, and code standardization. At present, interested readers may obtain the code from the corresponding author upon request.
Q12. Line 953. I don’t think I understand Fig. 1b. Why is it allowable for this curve to not be monotonically increasing? As I read this, the series for concentric craters would predict less area with thickness <6.5m than <5m, which doesn’t seem logical. For reference, I think this figure is a little like observational data akin to Fig. 6 of Hirabayashi et al. 2018 (though perhaps with axes switched). I would find it useful to have this translated into a best estimate for the regolith cfd/sfd (areal fraction with thickness <X or =X or >X or whatever).
This is a good question. In principle, the cumulative distribution of regolith thickness should be monotonic. If the spatial distribution of regolith thickness were known, the calculated cumulative distribution would necessarily be monotonic. For example, the figure below shows the monotonic cumulative distributions of regolith thickness derived from the models of Oberbeck et al. (1973), Hirabayashi et al. (2018), and Zhang et al. (2023b).
However, the cumulative regolith thickness inferred from crater morphology is obtained based on the proportion of craters with different morphologies within each diameter bin. It can be regarded as a random sampling of the underlying distribution, and therefore exhibits fluctuations depending on the number of crater samples. Ideally, with a sufficient number of fresh craters, the percentage of normal craters should decrease with diameter, whereas that of concentric craters should increase, resulting in a monotonic regolith thickness distribution (as an example, see Figs. 9 and 11 in Fa et al., 2014, JGR-Planets, 119, 1914–1935). In practice, however, the limited number of observed fresh craters leads to statistical fluctuations. For example, in a small diameter range D to D , if 90% of craters are concentric, the regolith thickness in 90% of the area is estimated to be <D/(9±0.6). In the next larger bin D to D , there may be only 80% concentric craters, implying only 80% of the area having regolith thickness <D /(9±0.6), which appears somewhat counterintuitive.
Similar behavior has been reported in Fig. 10 of Oberbeck & Quaide, (1968), Icarus, 9(1–3), 446–465, and Extended Data Fig. 4 in Xie et al., (2021), Nature Astronomy, 5(2), 128–133.
Here Fig. 1b is actually a cumulative frequency distribution that includes sampling uncertainty, which explains why the areal fraction with thickness <X is not strictly monotonic. Considering this, we adopt the result calculated from normal craters as the best estimate of median regolith thickness due to its smaller uncertainty. In the revision, we briefly explained the non-monotonic behavior. See L437–439.
Q13. Line 991. This figure is pretty cool…nice work.
Thank you.
Q14. Suppl. Figure 2, 4. I’ll note that these look sort of like Vanga et al.’s Fig 3 median regolith thicknesses, though probably with some difference in the values.
Yes. The median regolith thickness in Vange’s Fig. 3 was calculated based on the regolith growth model of Hirabayashi et al. 2018 JGR-Planets 123, 527–543. In our previous study, we compared the results of our analytical regolith growth model and Hirabayashi et al. (2018), and the general trends are similar (Fig. 10 in Zhang et al. 2023a JGR-Planets, 128, e2023JE007850).
